standard.title: Society Influencing Scientific Research
standard.description: examine how the values and needs of society influence the focus of scientific research
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined how scientific knowledge is used to make decisions (5-6 band). They now examine the reverse direction: how social values and needs shape what science is pursued in the first place.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how funding decisions, social priorities, ethical values and community needs direct scientific research — and examine the tensions and consequences that arise when research agendas are shaped by social rather than purely scientific priorities.

nodes.label: Social values and needs direct research priorities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how governments, communities and industries direct scientific research through funding and priority-setting, and identify how social values — including ethical constraints — shape what research is pursued.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two cases where social values or needs influenced the direction of scientific research, explaining the value or need and how it shaped the research focus.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine how government funding priorities, ethical constraints, public health needs and commercial interests shape research directions; explain how the need to minimise greenhouse gas production has directed both scientific and technological development; and examine how social priorities (safety, health, environmental sustainability) create research agendas.
wider: Research how First Nations Peoples of the Torres Strait are at the forefront of developing scientific measures to prevent transfer of infectious diseases — examining how community need directly shapes a specific research focus
Explore how Australia developed an AI system to predict IVF embryo viability — examining how medical need, technological capability and social values aligned to drive this research
Examine why many manufacturers are adopting green chemistry processes — connecting commercial, regulatory and environmental value systems to research and development priorities
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to examine tensions and negative consequences arising from socially-directed research. Students who only hold a benign model (community need → useful science) cannot engage critically with cases where directing values produced harm or contested outcomes — they lack the analytical frame Node 2 depends on.

response_modes.reason: Students readily identify funding and policy as drivers of research direction without seeing the variety of value systems — commercial, ethical, community, ideological — that shape research priorities. Encountering varied cases (community health need, commercial interest, government environmental priority, historical ideological constraint) builds a more complete model of the social-to-research pathway and prepares the critical analytical frame needed for Node 2.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Torres Strait community-directed research provides a powerful example of community values directly shaping scientific priorities, with contemporary relevance. The IVF AI direction shows how multiple value systems (medical, commercial, ethical) converge to create a specific research agenda.
success_criteria: Describes at least two cases where social values or needs influenced research direction
Explains the mechanism in each case — how the value or need translated into a specific research priority or constraint

nodes.label: Tensions and consequences arise when society shapes research
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the tensions and consequences that arise when research is shaped by social values and needs — including cases where values have directed research toward harm, and cases where research priorities are contested.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least one tension or negative consequence that has arisen from socially-directed research, and explain how the values or needs involved produced that outcome.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine contested research priorities (greenhouse gas minimisation vs economic growth; genetic testing vs privacy); examine a historical case where social values directed research toward harm; and explain how identifying whose values are shaping research is itself an important analytical move.
wider: Examine how considering innovative energy transfer devices reflects societal needs around transport and communication — exploring the values embedded in technology research priorities
Consider how development of new materials and procedures for workplace sound safety reflects occupational health values — examining how community wellbeing shapes materials research

Research how 19th and early 20th century Australian social values and scientific misconceptions about heredity influenced policies and attitudes toward First Nations Australians — examining how harmful values can direct harmful research (connects to AC9S10H04)

response_modes.reason: Students readily see socially-directed research as benign (community need → useful science) without examining cases where the directing values produced harm or contested outcomes. Making the analytical move explicit — whose values are shaping this research? what are the consequences? — is the scaffold that produces critical rather than descriptive engagement with the science-society relationship.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one tension or contested priority in a socially-directed research case
Explains how the values or needs that shaped the research direction produced the tension or consequence
